topic: Day 1 · Risk Stratification — Blatchford, Rockall & AIMS65
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Same-Day Emergency Care & GI Bleed Unit
speakerBio: A gastroenterologist who built the hospital's GI-bleed triage pathway and is evangelical that the safest thing you can do for a low-risk patient is let them go home — and the safest thing for a high-risk one is to score them and believe it.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start — two patients, one waiting room

Two patients arrive within an hour. The first: a 24-year-old who vomited once after a heavy night, saw "a streak of red," now completely well — HR 72, BP 124/78, urea normal, Hb 148, no melaena, no comorbidity. The second: a 78-year-old on aspirin with melaena, HR 108, systolic 104, urea 14, Hb 88. Both are "GI bleeds." One can walk out of the department today; the other needs an urgent scope and a bed. The skill that separates them is not a scan or a scope — it is a score. Risk stratification is how you spend the right resource on the right patient at the right time.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

Risk scores answer two questions the eye cannot: "Can this patient safely go home?" and "How fast does this patient need a scope?" Blatchford triages the front door; Rockall predicts the outcome; AIMS65 is the fast bedside mortality flag.

These are the three scores of upper GI bleeding. They are not academic — they drive disposition (home vs admit) and timing of endoscopy. Used well, they turn a chaotic queue into a triaged, evidence-based flow.

2 · The Glasgow–Blatchford Score (GBS) — the "can they go home?" score 🚪

The GBS is a pre-endoscopy, purely clinical score — it uses only admission blood tests and observations, no endoscopic findings and no age term. Its great strength is at the low end: it identifies patients so low-risk they can be managed as outpatients.

ComponentValues & points
Blood urea (mmol/L)6.5–8 (+2), 8–10 (+3), 10–25 (+4), ≥25 (+6)
Haemoglobin — men (g/L)120–130 (+1), 100–120 (+3), <100 (+6)
Haemoglobin — women (g/L)100–120 (+1), <100 (+6)
Systolic BP (mmHg)100–109 (+1), 90–99 (+2), <90 (+3)
Other markersPulse ≥100 (+1); melaena (+1); syncope (+2); liver disease (+2); cardiac failure (+2)
💡 The number that sends a patient home

A Glasgow–Blatchford score of 0 (or ≤1) identifies a very-low-risk patient with a minimal chance of needing intervention (transfusion, endoscopic therapy, surgery) or dying. These patients can be considered for outpatient management — no admission, and endoscopy as an outpatient rather than an emergency. ACG 2021 and NICE both endorse this. To score 0, the patient must have essentially everything normal: normal urea and Hb, systolic ≥110, pulse <100, no melaena, no syncope, no liver or cardiac disease.

🎯 What to DO with the GBS

GBS 0–1: very low risk → consider discharge with outpatient endoscopy. GBS ≥ 2 (and especially ≥7): admit; higher scores predict greater need for intervention and earlier endoscopy. The GBS is best thought of as the rule-out tool — it is highly sensitive at the low end, so a 0 is genuinely reassuring, whereas a high score flags "this patient will need something."

3 · The Rockall Score — the "how bad is the outcome?" score 📉

Rockall predicts rebleeding and mortality. It comes in two forms, and the distinction matters:

  • Pre-endoscopic (clinical / admission) Rockall — uses age, shock (pulse & BP), and comorbidity only. Available before the scope.
  • Full (complete) Rockall — adds the two endoscopic variables: the diagnosis and the stigmata of recent haemorrhage. Only completable after endoscopy.
Variable0123
Age<6060–79≥80—
ShockNone (SBP≥100, HR<100)HR≥100 (SBP≥100)SBP<100—
ComorbidityNone major—Cardiac failure, IHDRenal/liver failure, metastatic cancer
Diagnosis (endoscopic)Mallory–Weiss / no lesionAll other diagnosesUpper GI malignancy—
Stigmata of recent haemorrhage (endoscopic)None / dark spot—Blood, adherent clot, visible/spurting vessel—

The two endoscopic rows are why the full Rockall cannot be completed until after the scope — and why it is a better predictor of outcome than the clinical score alone.

Full Rockall scoreApprox. rebleedingApprox. mortality
0–2 (low)~5%~0–2%
3–4 (intermediate)~11–14%~5–10%
≥5 (high)~25–40%+~17–40%+
🎯 What to DO with Rockall

A pre-endoscopic Rockall of 0 also identifies a low-risk group. A full Rockall ≤ 2 after endoscopy predicts low rebleeding and mortality — supporting early discharge. A full Rockall ≥ 5 flags a high-risk patient who needs close monitoring, a low threshold for repeat endoscopy, and often ICU-level care. Rockall is the prognostic score — it tells you how worried to be, before and after the scope.

4 · AIMS65 — the fast mortality flag ⚡

AIMS65 is a simple, quick score built to predict in-hospital mortality. It is an easy mnemonic of five equally weighted, readily available variables — one point each:

LetterVariableThreshold (1 point)
AAlbumin< 30 g/L
IINR> 1.5
MAltered Mental statusPresent (e.g. GCS < 14)
SSystolic BP≤ 90 mmHg
65Age≥ 65 years

Mortality climbs steeply with score: roughly <1% at 0, rising to ~20–25%+ at 4–5. AIMS65 is excellent at predicting death and is fast to calculate at the bedside; it is less focused than Blatchford at identifying the discharge-safe patient.

💡 One-liner — which score for which question

Blatchford = "Can they go home?" (best at the low-risk end, no endoscopy needed). Rockall = "How likely to rebleed or die?" (pre- and post-endoscopic prognosis). AIMS65 = "How likely to die?" (fast bedside mortality). Pick the tool to fit the decision in front of you.

5 · How the scores drive disposition & timing 🧭

This is the whole point — turning a number into an action:

Risk tierTypical scoresDispositionEndoscopy timing
Very lowGBS 0–1; pre-endoscopic Rockall 0Home from ED / SDECOutpatient (non-urgent)
Low–intermediateGBS 2–6; full Rockall 0–2Admit, wardWithin 24 h of presentation (early endoscopy)
HighGBS ≥7; full Rockall ≥5; AIMS65 ≥2Admit, high-dependency / ICU considerationEarly (within 24 h) once resuscitated; urgent if unstable/ongoing
Unstable / ongoing haemorrhagePersisting shock despite resuscitationResus → ICUEmergent — after resuscitation, do not delay
The score does not replace judgement — it disciplines it. A low score plus a worried gut still earns a second look; a high score is a mandate to act, not a suggestion.
🎯 Contrast — who goes home vs who needs the urgent scope

Goes home: young, well, normal urea and Hb, no melaena, no syncope, no comorbidity, systolic ≥110, pulse <100 → GBS 0 → outpatient endoscopy. Needs urgent scope + admission: shocked, melaena, high urea, low Hb, elderly, comorbid, altered mental state → high GBS / Rockall / AIMS65 → resuscitate then early (≤24 h) or emergent endoscopy. Same complaint, opposite pathways — the score is the switch.

6 · The limits — what scores don't do ⚠️

  • Scores are decision aids, not decision-makers. Clinical deterioration overrides any reassuring number.
  • The GBS can be falsely low if urea and Hb have not yet moved (very early presentation) — trend, don't snapshot.
  • They are validated for upper GI bleeding; lower GI scores (e.g. Oakland) are separate.
  • A normal score does not mean "no endoscopy ever" — it means "not emergently."
☠️ M&M — "The score said low risk"

A 71-year-old woman on apixaban attended with one episode of coffee-ground vomiting. Early bloods: urea 6.0, Hb 118, systolic 112, pulse 92 — a junior calculated a Glasgow–Blatchford of 1 and, reassured by "very low risk," arranged discharge with an outpatient scope. What was missed: her presentation was only two hours old (urea and Hb had not yet risen), she was anticoagulated, and she had melaena on PR that had not been recorded in the score. Six hours later she re-presented shocked with a large haematemesis from a posterior duodenal ulcer eroding the gastroduodenal artery. Review found the GBS had been applied mechanically to a patient whose risk factors (anticoagulation, very early presentation, an unrecorded melaena point) made the low score unreliable. Lessons: (1) A GBS of 0–1 is safe for discharge only when the whole clinical picture agrees — score the melaena, count the anticoagulant, distrust the very early snapshot. (2) Scores triage; they do not overrule a concerning story. (3) When in doubt, observe and rescore rather than discharge.

7 · Take-home 🎯

  • Glasgow–Blatchford is the pre-endoscopic clinical score; a GBS of 0–1 = very low risk, safe for outpatient management (no admission, outpatient scope).
  • Rockall predicts rebleeding and mortality: pre-endoscopic (age, shock, comorbidity) vs full (adds endoscopic diagnosis + stigmata). Full ≤2 = low risk; ≥5 = high risk.
  • AIMS65 (Albumin<30, INR>1.5, Mental status, SBP≤90, age≥65) is a fast bedside mortality flag.
  • Scores drive disposition (home vs admit) and timing (outpatient vs ≤24 h vs emergent).
  • Most stable admitted patients get endoscopy within 24 hours; unstable ongoing bleeders get it emergently after resuscitation.
  • Scores discipline judgement — they never replace it. Distrust a low score in an anticoagulated patient or a very early presentation.

Next session: while the patient waits for that scope, what can pharmacology do to buy time and improve the odds? PPIs, prokinetics, and the life-saving variceal bundle.

moderatorQs.q: What makes the Glasgow–Blatchford score particularly suited to the front door, and what does a score of 0 actually permit you to do?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The Glasgow–Blatchford score is purely clinical and pre-endoscopic — it uses only admission observations and bloods (urea, haemoglobin, systolic BP, pulse, melaena, syncope, liver disease, cardiac failure) with no endoscopic data and no age term, so it can be calculated the moment the patient arrives. Its power is at the low-risk end: it is highly sensitive for identifying patients who will need no intervention. A GBS of 0 (or ≤1) identifies a very-low-risk patient who can be considered for outpatient management — discharge without admission and endoscopy as an outpatient — a recommendation endorsed by ACG 2021 and NICE. To score 0 the patient needs a normal urea and Hb, systolic ≥110, pulse <100, and no melaena, syncope, liver or cardiac disease. It is the rule-out tool of upper GI bleeding.

moderatorQs.q: Distinguish the pre-endoscopic Rockall score from the full Rockall score, and explain why the distinction matters clinically.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The pre-endoscopic (clinical) Rockall uses only age, shock (pulse and blood pressure), and comorbidity — it is available at admission and gives an early prognostic estimate. The full Rockall adds the two endoscopic variables — the diagnosis (e.g. malignancy scores higher, Mallory–Weiss lower) and the stigmata of recent haemorrhage (a visible or spurting vessel or adherent clot scores high) — so it can only be completed after the scope. The distinction matters because the full score is a better predictor of rebleeding and mortality: a full Rockall of ≤2 predicts low rebleeding (~5%) and mortality and supports early discharge, whereas ≥5 predicts high rebleeding and mortality (upwards of 25–40%) and mandates close monitoring, a low threshold for repeat endoscopy, and higher-level care. Rockall is fundamentally the prognostic score, before and after endoscopy.

moderatorQs.q: How do these scores translate into the timing of endoscopy for an admitted patient versus one who is unstable?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: For the stable admitted patient, the evidence and ACG 2021 support endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation ('early' endoscopy) after adequate resuscitation — this is the standard for the great majority. A very-low-risk patient (GBS 0–1) does not need inpatient endoscopy at all and can have it as an outpatient. At the other extreme, the patient who remains haemodynamically unstable with ongoing haemorrhage despite resuscitation needs emergent endoscopy — you resuscitate first and then scope without delay, often in a monitored/ICU setting. So the scores stratify a spectrum: home with outpatient scope → admit for endoscopy within 24 h → resuscitate and scope emergently. Importantly, very early emergent endoscopy is reserved for instability; routinely rushing a stabilised patient to a scope in under 12 hours has not been shown to improve outcomes and can be counterproductive.

audienceQs.q: A young patient with a small haematemesis has a Glasgow–Blatchford score of 0. Can I really send them home without a scope in the department?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes — that is exactly what the score is designed to permit, provided the whole picture agrees. A GBS of 0 (or ≤1) marks a very-low-risk patient whose chance of needing transfusion, endoscopic therapy or dying is minimal, so they can be discharged for an outpatient endoscopy rather than admitted for an emergency one (ACG 2021 / NICE). But confirm the score is genuinely 0: normal urea and haemoglobin, systolic ≥110, pulse <100, and crucially no melaena, no syncope, no liver or cardiac disease. Beware the very early presentation (urea and Hb may not have risen yet) and the anticoagulated patient — in those, a low score can be falsely reassuring, so observe and rescore rather than discharge. When the score and the story disagree, believe the story.

audienceQs.q: There are three scores. In practice, do I need all of them, or is one enough?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Use the score that fits the decision. For the front-door 'can this patient go home?' decision, use the Glasgow–Blatchford — it is the best-validated rule-out tool and needs no endoscopy. For prognosis — rebleeding and mortality — use Rockall, the pre-endoscopic version at admission and the full version after the scope. AIMS65 is a quick, five-variable mortality flag (Albumin<30, INR>1.5, altered Mental status, SBP≤90, age≥65) that is easy to calculate at the bedside. In most units the GBS drives triage and disposition, and Rockall (or AIMS65) informs how worried to be and the level of monitoring. You do not mechanically compute all three on everyone — you reach for the one that answers your current question, and let clinical deterioration override any of them.
